papers.title_in_file: Time-dependent Hamiltonians and Geometry of Operators Generated by Them
papers.version_note: arXiv v2, 21 Jul 2025; the text layer replaces italic math symbols with a replacement character, so formulas are quoted in words.
papers.not_read: Equation symbols and figure plots lost in the text layer; captions and surrounding text were read.
papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that computes the bi-invariant Nielsen cost of time evolution under time-dependent oscillator Hamiltonians, with an equivalence between two oscillator models, a bound, and a quench example.

assertions.value: The authors state that they compute the bi-invariant cost associated with explicitly time-dependent Hamiltonians, using Nielsen's geometric formulation of circuit complexity and a regularisation of the norm.
quotes: Using Nielsen’s geometric formulation of circuit complexity, we calculate the bi-invariant cost associated with these time-dependent Hamiltonians by suitably regularising their norms
assertions.certainty_reason: The abstract states the scope of the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantity they compute is the total cost along the specified time-evolution curve, not a minimum over curves, because the curve generated by a time-dependent Hamiltonian is not a geodesic of the bi-invariant geometry.
assertions.anchor: Section I, p.3 and Section V E, p.19
quotes: Therefore, in this set-up it is only meaningful to consider the total cost along the given curve, not the minimum among a set of such costs
since the specified curve is not a geodesic of the biinvariant geometry, this cost is not the minimum one, i.e., it does not correspond to the complexity of the given operator
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope and the status of the quantity it computes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamiltonians treated have explicit time dependence and an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, and that all systems considered are one-dimensional.
assertions.anchor: Section I p.3; Section III p.7
quotes: explicit time dependence and infinite-dimensional Hilbert space
considered in this paper are one-dimensional.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated scope of the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that requiring bi-invariance of the complexity geometry gives a class of cost functions that is the Schatten norm, and that the paper uses the case where the cost is the trace of the squared Hamiltonian, which is a length on the Cartan-Killing metric of the Lie group.
assertions.anchor: Section II p.6 and Section III p.6
quotes: The resulting cost function is known as the Schatten norm.

the bi-invariant cost represents a length on a Riemannian metric, which is nothing but the Cartan-Killing metric corresponding to the Lie group whose generator is the Hamiltonian of the quantum system
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the cost used throughout.

assertions.value: The authors attribute the proposal of bi-invariant complexity to earlier work, on the grounds that Nielsen complexity geometries of two unitarily related Hamiltonians would otherwise differ.
quotes: the notion of bi-invariant complexity was proposed in [39–41]
assertions.certainty_reason: Attributed to cited work.

assertions.value: The authors state that even after imposing smoothness, continuity, positivity, positive homogeneity and the triangle inequality, the cost function in Nielsen's approach is not unique.
quotes: However, even after imposing all these requirements on the cost, it is not unique.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states this limit of the framework.

assertions.value: The authors define a regularisation in which a mean value, a multiple of the identity, is subtracted from the Hamiltonian so that the zeta-regularised trace of the displaced Hamiltonian vanishes, and they call this the regularization condition. They state that the subtraction does not alter the complexity geometry.
quotes: We refer to this condition as the regularization condition in the following.
A procedure of obtaining the CG by suitably regularizing the trace of the Hamiltonian operator using the Hurwitz
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition of the regularisation used.
assertions.reader_inference: The regularisation originates in a cited earlier work (their reference 41), which the paper reviews.

assertions.value: The authors state that for time-independent Hamiltonians the geodesic is generated by a constant generator, so the regularised norm gives the complexity of the operator.
quotes: the geodesic is generated by a constant generator [50] - here the Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated consequence of bi-invariance, with a textbook reference.

assertions.value: The authors state that an extra constant linear driving force in a generalised-oscillator Hamiltonian can be interpreted as a trace regulator, and that it does not change the quantitative value of the cost.
quotes: In that section we also show how the addition of an extra linear force term in the Hamiltonian can be interpreted as a trace regulator
the constant force term ������0 does not change the quantitative value of the cost
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Appendix A 1.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the isotonic oscillator the regularisation mean value can be positive as well as negative, depending on the strength of the singular term, unlike the harmonic oscillator case.
quotes: can be positive as well as negative.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the regularisation condition in Appendix A 2.

assertions.value: The authors state that for a harmonic oscillator with time-dependent frequency, using the Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant operator eigenfunctions, they obtain a compact analytical formula for the regularised cost function, and they call it one of the main results of the paper.
assertions.anchor: Introduction p.4; Section IV C, p.11
quotes: we obtain a compact analytical formula for the regularised cost function (see eq. (47))
This constitutes one of the main results of the present paper.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Section IV; the formula is stated as Eq. (47). The symbols of the formula are lost in the text layer, so only the paper's statement is quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that a time-dependent Hamiltonian has no stationary eigenstates, so both diagonal and non-diagonal matrix elements in a suitable basis are required for the cost, and that the non-diagonal contribution reduces the total cost for a normal oscillator with real frequency.
assertions.anchor: Section VII p.23; Section IV C p.11
quotes: since a time-dependent Hamiltonian has no stationary eigenstates, both diagonal as well as non-diagonal matrix elements of this Hamiltonian in a suitable basis are required for the computation of the cost
is to reduce the total cost
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the derivation of the norm in Section IV C.

assertions.value: The authors state that the sign ambiguity of the regularisation constant is resolved by requiring that the norm reduce to the harmonic oscillator result in the limit of constant frequency, which selects the negative value.
quotes: We can resolve this ambiguity by imposing the natural condition
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the condition it imposes.
assertions.reader_inference: The choice of sign is therefore imposed by a matching condition, not derived.

assertions.value: The authors state that in the limit of constant frequency the second term of the cost vanishes and the cost is proportional to the square of the frequency of the harmonic oscillator.
quotes: so that the second term in the (first expression of the) cost in Eq. (47) vanishes, and we recover the result obtained in [41], i.e., that the cost is proportional to the square of the frequency of a HO
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit of the derived formula.

assertions.value: The authors prove, with the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality for square-integrable functions, an upper bound on the total cost up to a finite time. They state that the bound is proportional to the square root of the time average of the square of the expectation value of the Hamiltonian in the lowest quantum state of the oscillator.
assertions.anchor: Section IV C, Eqs. (50) and (51), p.12
quotes: We now derive an interesting bound on the total cost of the time evolution by using the CauchySchwarz inequality for square-integrable functions.

Therefore, the upper bound of the total cost is proportional to the square root of time average of the square of the expectation value of the Hamiltonian in the lowest quantum state of the oscillator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Eq. (50); the explicit bound is Eq. (51), whose symbols are lost in the text layer, so the statement is quoted in words.

assertions.value: The authors state that the upper bound can be formally inverted to give a lower bound on the time required to reach a given value of total cost, and that such an inequality often appears in the context of the quantum speed limit.
quotes: we can also formally invert the above expression to obtain a lower bound on the time required to reach a given value of total cost
Inequality such as this often appears in the context of the quantum speed limit
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as a formal inversion; the quantum-speed-limit link is an analogy the paper only mentions.

assertions.value: The authors report that for a frequency profile of the form one over a linear function of time, in one parameter range, the norm of the Hamiltonian is proportional to the square of the time-dependent frequency, and that it goes to zero at infinite time where the Hamiltonian becomes that of a free particle.
quotes: Therefore, the norm of the Hamiltonian is proportional to the square of the time-dependent frequency
making the Hamiltonian that of a free particle, so that the norm also goes to zero in that limit
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived analytically in Eq. (55) for this profile.

assertions.value: The authors report that for this frequency profile the total cost along the time-evolution curve grows logarithmically for large time, and is proportional to the average frequency of the oscillator.
quotes: Therefore, for large values of time, the total cost evaluated along the time evolution curve grows logarithmically.
Here the total cost is actually proportional to the average frequency of the oscillator.
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived by integrating the norm in Eq. (56).

assertions.value: The authors report that for the borderline parameter case of the same profile the norm is proportional to the square of the frequency but its time dependence is not solely given by the frequency, and that the total cost expression is lengthy and not reproduced.
quotes: the time dependence is not solely given by the frequency
An analytical expression for the total cost can be calculated as before, though this expression is quite lengthy
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated outcome of the derivation in Eq. (58).

assertions.value: The authors report that when the Schwarzian derivative vanishes the norm is not entirely proportional to the frequency, and that it is proportional only when an integration constant vanishes.
assertions.anchor: Section IV E, p.13 and footnote 9, p.13
quotes: the expression for the norm is not entirely proportional to the time-dependent frequency.
The norm is proportional to the frequency
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Eq. (60).

assertions.value: The authors state that the generalised time-dependent oscillator is related to an oscillator with time-dependent mass and frequency by a time-independent unitary transformation, so the norms are equal, and that for a unitary transformation that is a function of time the bi-invariant cost would no longer be invariant.
quotes: For a unitary transformation, which is a general function of time, the bi-invariant cost would no longer be invariant.
due to unitary invariance of the CG in Eq. (11), the norms of both the Hamiltonians are equivalent
assertions.certainty_reason: Follows from the invariance of the cost under time-independent unitaries.

assertions.value: The authors state that they obtain an analytical expression for the regularised cost of the oscillator with time-dependent mass and frequency, and a bound on its total cost analogous to the one for the time-dependent frequency oscillator.
assertions.anchor: Section V A, Eqs. (74) and (76), p.15
quotes: In this case we can derive a bound on the total cost by following a similar procedure as in section IV C
we have obtained compact analytical expressions for the cost of the time evolution operator generated by these two Hamiltonians (see eqs. (47) and (74), respectively)
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Section V A; the symbols of the formulas are lost in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Hamiltonian of the oscillator with time-dependent mass and frequency is an element of a Lie algebra written with the label (1, 1), so its time-evolution operator is an element of the corresponding group and can be written in two equivalent forms.
quotes: First we notice that the Hamiltonian in (63) is an element of the ������������(1, 1) Lie algebra.
The fact that the Hamiltonian is an element of the ������������(1, 1) algebra naturally indicates that the corresponding time evolution operator is an element of the
assertions.certainty_reason: Shown by the commutation relations in Eq. (79).

assertions.value: The authors show that under a redefinition of the time parameter the Schrodinger equation, auxiliary equation, wave functions and time-evolution operator of the oscillator with time-dependent mass and frequency map to those of a unit-mass oscillator with time-dependent frequency.
assertions.anchor: Section V C, Eqs. (84) to (91), pp.17-18
quotes: This completes our demonstration that under the reparametrisation of time two systems, an OTMF and an OTF are equivalent.
the Schrodinger equation for an OTMF with mass
assertions.certainty_reason: Demonstrated in Section V C; the conditions and the reparametrisation are Eq. (84), whose symbols are lost in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors show that the total bi-invariant cost of creating a given operator along the time-evolution curve is the same whether it is generated by the oscillator with time-dependent mass and frequency or by the unit-mass oscillator with time-dependent frequency, under the time reparametrisation of Eq. (84).
quotes: Having established that under the change of time parameter given by Eq. (84), different quantities associated with two sys-
is equal to the total cost when it is generated by the Hamiltonian
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived in Eq. (94); the integrands of the two costs map into each other under the reparametrisation.

assertions.value: The authors state that the equivalence of total costs is not an artifact of the unitary invariance of the cost function, and that the two Hamiltonians are not related by any time-independent unitary transformation.
quotes: The total costs are equivalent even if the two Hamiltonians are not related by any timeindependent unitary transformation.
the two Hamiltonians in question (an OTF and OTMF) are not related by any time-independent unitary transformation
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated with the derivation in Section V D.

assertions.value: The authors state that the norms of the two Hamiltonians do not map to each other under the reparametrisation, only their integrals do, and that the upper bounds on the total cost do not map to each other either.
quotes: the norms of the two Hamiltonians do not map to each other under the said transformation
the upper bounds on the total cost functions in eqs. (51) and (76) do not map to each other under time reparametrisation
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated by the authors as a limit of the equivalence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two Hamiltonians can be connected by time-dependent unitary transformations, and that for that reason their bi-invariant costs would not be equivalent through those transformations.
quotes: However, these unitary transformations are time-dependent, and therefore, the bi-invariant costs of these two Hamiltonians are not equivalent.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated limit of bi-invariance.

assertions.value: The authors state that the minimum cost, the complexity, is obtained along the geodesic, which is generated by a constant Hamiltonian, and that for the oscillator curve this constant generator is a generalised oscillator with constant coefficients.
quotes: In fact, the minimum cost i.e., the complexity, is obtained by evaluating the cost along the geodesic, which, according to the bi-invariance, is generated by a constant Hamiltonian.
This is just the Hamiltonian of a generalised oscillator with constant coefficients considered in section III
assertions.certainty_reason: Derived from the time-evolution operator at the end point.

assertions.value: The authors propose, as future work, an efficiency of the evolution defined as the ratio of the geodesic distance to the length of the path generated by the time-dependent Hamiltonian, using the bi-invariant geometry.
quotes: It will be interesting to study this quantity further in a future work.
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated open direction.

assertions.value: The authors state that they study a frequency profile for a smooth quench, the end-critical protocol, in which the oscillator frequency is constant up to the initial time and then decreases continuously toward zero in the limit of infinite time.
quotes: Quantum quenches where the frequency exhibits this kind of time dependence are known as the end-critical protocol in the literature.
after which the frequency of the oscillator is changed continuously with time from a maximum value at

assertions.value: The authors report, citing a recent observation, that the change in Shannon entropy before and after the start of the quench does not depend on the state label. They report that in the adiabatic regime before the Kibble-Zurek time the change is approximated by an adiabatic formula and that at large time it takes a fixed constant value predicted accurately by that formula.
assertions.anchor: Section VI A, p.20-21 and Fig. 1
quotes: From the exact result it can be seen that for relatively small values of ������, the change in SE grows and then shows oscillatory behavior, however these oscillations dry out quickly

assertions.reader_inference: The state-independence of the entropy change is attributed to a cited work; the quoted text states the oscillations dry out.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the quench the cost grows quadratically at small dimensionless time and then linearly. They report that its behaviour for the larger parameter regime depends on the parameter value, and that at the start of the quench it equals the constant-frequency harmonic oscillator value.

quotes: Therefore, unlike the change in the SE, the cost
does not saturate to a constant value for large
assertions.certainty_reason: Read from plots and an approximate expansion.
assertions.reader_inference: The same section also says that, at fixed values of one parameter, the cost takes constant values at late times; the text layer loses the symbols, so which parameter is held fixed in each statement cannot be checked here.

assertions.value: The authors state that the constants that multiply the two terms of the cost come from numerical factors, with the second constant including the value of a generalised Epstein-Hurwitz series, and that only their overall magnitude, not the time dependence, is affected by them.

quotes: What we need here to evaluate the cost is the numerical value of this series for
they only affect the overall magnitude of the norm, not its time dependence

assertions.value: The authors report that for the damped Caldirola-Kanai oscillator the bi-invariant cost function is independent of time even though the Hamiltonian is explicitly time dependent, because its matrix elements are time independent in the invariant-operator basis. They state that this is not true in general and that the cost is not the minimum.

of the CK Hamiltonian are time-independent in the basis of the invariant operator eigenfunctions.

papers.title_in_file: Bayesian Networks Are Not the Solution to Opening Machine Learning’s Black Box
papers.what_it_is: A short position paper by two Cycorp authors arguing that Bayesian networks are limited as a transparent alternative to black-box machine learning, and that Cyc and CycL are the better solution.

assertions.value: The authors define a Bayesian network as a graphical representation of probability distributions with three components: nodes, directed edges and probabilities. Each node represents a proposition that fixes the value of some variable.
quotes: a Bayesian network is a graphical representation of probability distributions. There are three components:
Each node in a Bayesian network graph represents a proposition that ﬁxes the value of some variable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition of a Bayesian network in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors state Bayes' Theorem as P(A|B) = P(A)*P(B|A)/P(B), as long as P(B) is nonzero, and say that updating a single node of a completed graph ripples forward and backward through the arrows to give posterior probabilities for each node.
quotes: Bayes’ Theorem states that P(A—B) = P(A)*P(B—A)/P(B), as long as P(B) is nonzero.
updating the status of a single node will ripple forward and backward through the arrows and generate posterior probabilities for each node.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard result stated without proof; the vertical bar is printed as an em dash by the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer prints the conditioning bar as an em dash.

assertions.value: The authors state that a Bayesian network can be inspected so that the step by step path from the givens to a conclusion is read off as an explanation, that experts can enter the nodes and connections, and that it can work from a small amount of data or none.
quotes: The resulting graph can be inspected and processed so as to provide a kind of explanation for each conclusion that it draws.
It could even be the case that experts were used to enter the nodes in the graph and their connections.
only requiring a relatively small amount of data (or even no data) to work.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argued claim illustrated by a rain and wet ground example; no experiment.

assertions.value: The authors state that Bayesian networks are more transparent than a purely statistical ML black box such as a multi-layer neural network, because a node's conditional probability tables can be at least partially examined. They state that neural nets require big data and have opaque methods.
quotes: Bayesian networks are more transparent than a purely statistical ML black box
Neural nets use complex math to churn out predictive correlations, but they require big data, and their methods are opaque.
you can at least
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without measurement.
assertions.reader_inference: The quote 'you can at least' ends page 4 and the sentence continues on page 5 with 'partially examine this causal model'.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as far as the reasoning method is concerned, there is only ever one type of link in a given Bayesian network graph, and that links are therefore often interpreted as causal. They state that a graph that mixes several meanings of a link makes its conclusion difficult to understand and to trust.
quotes: The problem is that so far as the reasoning method (ii, above) is concerned, there is only ever one type of link in a given Bayesian network graph.
Thus, links in a Bayesian network are often interpreted as causal.
which makes the conclusion diﬃcult to understand and diﬃcult to trust.
assertions.certainty_reason: An argued limitation stated without a formal proof.
assertions.reader_inference: This describes a typical Bayesian network formalism; the paper does not cite any work that allows typed links.

assertions.value: The authors give examples of Bayesian network links that are not causal. The link from having a male sibling to having a brother is definitional. The link between a woman being in a hospital and having a newborn infant reflects a common cause, giving birth.
quotes: But a link between “a person has a male sibling” to “a person has a brother” is deﬁnitional, not causal.
Instead, we know that there is a common cause for both: giving birth.
assertions.certainty_reason: Illustrative examples chosen by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors describe a product recommendation example in which a link from a person having a friend who owns a product to that person enjoying it is ambiguous, either causal or less causal. They state that a graph with six nodes can separate the readings, but that there is no uniform interpretation of what a link means, because some links are better characterized as semantic links.
quotes: Since there are no graphs with diﬀerent types of links, the simple graph we just built is impoverished in the explanations it can generate.
but there is no uniform interpretation of what a link means.
Those links are better characterized as semantic links between nodes.
assertions.certainty_reason: A worked illustration by the authors, with no data.
assertions.reader_inference: The six-node figure is partly lost in the text layer, so only the surrounding text was read.

assertions.value: The authors state that the number of conditional probabilities to be calculated is exponential in the number of parents of a node. They state that the node 'A is interested in C' has 5 parents, so its conditional probability table for binary values needs 25 calculations, as printed with the exponent flat (two to the power of five).
quotes: The number of conditional probabilities that need to be counted is exponential given the number of parents that a node has.
The node ‘A is interested in C’ has 5 parents.
we would need to make 25 calculations.
assertions.certainty_reason: A stated counting argument for one example, not a theorem.
assertions.reader_inference: Two to the power of five is 32. The text layer prints it as 25, so the printed figure should be read as the exponent printed flat, not as twenty-five.

assertions.value: The authors illustrate scaling with a company of 200 customers, 300 products and 100 friends per customer. They state that the number of entries in the conditional probability table of one node would be 100200*300 as printed, with the exponent flat, and call it astronomical.
quotes: Suppose that the company has 200 customers and 300 products, and each customer could be friends with 100 people.
the number of entries in that node’s conditional probability table would be 100200*300.
That number is astronomical
assertions.certainty_reason: A back of envelope illustration with a mangled expression; not computed or run.
assertions.reader_inference: The printed expression is probably 100 to the power 200*300. The sentence describing the node (two parents, one taking friends as values) does not obviously match that exponent.

assertions.value: The authors state that Bayesian networks perform well on small graphs where nodes have a relatively small number of possible values. They state that there are ways to prevent the exponential growth, but that none would apply to the graph that ends in 'A is interested in C'.
quotes: Bayesian networks perform well on small graphs where nodes have a relatively small number of possible values.
Although there are ways to prevent this exponential growth, none of them would apply to the graph that concludes with ‘A is interested in C’.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the paper does not describe the ways to prevent the growth.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not name the techniques (for example structure restrictions or approximate inference) that it says do not apply.

assertions.value: The authors list gaps in Bayesian network transparency: the way the structure was determined is not always known and, if statistically derived, may be as much of a black box as a neural net. The way the conditional probabilities were determined is not always known and may be opaque if ML generated them. The explanations still bottom out in understanding a graphical model.
quotes: We will not always know how the structure was determined. If it was statistically derived, the structure itself may be as much of a black box as a neural net.
We will not always know how the conditional probabilities were determined.
These explanations still bottom out in being able to understand a graphical model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Author claims about limits of the approach, with no measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that Bayesian network inference leads to affirmative conclusions, and that plausible arguments against a conclusion Q are not generally computable and so cannot be read off and articulated. They say a satisfying explanation should give reasons that support a conclusion or argue against it.
quotes: plausible arguments against Q being true are not generally computable, and hence not capable of being “read oﬀ” and articulated.
A satisfying explanation should make clear the reasons that support a conclusion or argue against it.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim without proof.

assertions.value: The authors summarize that Bayesian networks are powerful tools for modeling clearly defined causal structures, but face issues of scalability, transparency, and pro and con argumentation.
quotes: Bayesian networks are powerful tools for modeling clearly deﬁned causal structures, but they face issues in terms of scalability, transparency, and pro/con argumentation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary of the authors' arguments, not a measured result.

assertions.value: The authors, who write for Cycorp, state that Cyc produces a series of reasons for every answer, that its rules are completely public with nothing hidden, and that it can look back at the successful path to give a step by step justification.
quotes: Cyc produces a series of reasons for every answer it generates.
The rules that Cyc uses are completely public; there is nothing hidden.
it can look back at the successful path to that answer in order to provide a step by step justiﬁcation for that answer.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor description of its own product, with no independent evaluation in the paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The authors are from the vendor of Cyc; the paper says it is Cycorp's view (see 'we translate' and 'Cycorp has a demonstrably scalable solution').

assertions.value: The authors report one example in which Cyc, asked whether fatigued lifeguards have trouble doing their job, answers that this is true and gives two supporting facts, one of which is not causal. They state that Cyc justifies the non-causal fact by two further facts about swimming being an athletic activity.
quotes: Do fatigued lifeguards have trouble doing their job?
Lifeguards have to be able to perform athletic activities for their jobs.
Swimming is an athletic activity.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's illustrative example of its own product, given without a transcript or a test set.
assertions.reader_inference: A single hand picked example does not measure how often Cyc's explanations are correct.

assertions.value: The authors state that all of Cyc's knowledge is fully explicit, declarative and reusable, and that Cyc can answer a new question from its knowledge base without a new graph and new conditional probabilities.
quotes: All of Cyc’s knowledge is fully explicit, declarative, and reusable.

instead of having to write a new graph and calculate new conditional probabilities for something that a Bayesian network has never encountered, Cyc can draw on its vast knowledge base to answer a question.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor description of its own product.

assertions.value: The authors report that Cyc knows 25,000,000 principles and rules of thumb, that its one-step inferences number in the trillions, and that explanation graphs with a small number of thousands of inference steps are not uncommon. A footnote states that Cyc uses just 0.001% of its knowledge for a specific question, which the authors compute as 2,500 steps.
quotes: It knows 25,000,000 principles and rules of thumb that it can leverage at any time
Even the number of one-step inferences Cyc can draw is in the trillions
0.001% of 25 million is 2,500
assertions.certainty_reason: Vendor figures about its own knowledge base; the paper does not say how they were counted.
assertions.reader_inference: The size of a knowledge base is not by itself a measure of inference speed or of accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that the size of Cyc's knowledge base is proof that it is scalable, and that over 35 years of experience developing applications on the same ever-growing knowledge base show that Cycorp has a demonstrably scalable solution.
quotes: expansive knowledge base is proof that it is scalable.
with over 35 years of experience developing a variety of applications that leverage the same (ever-growing) knowledge base, Cycorp has a demonstrably scalable solution.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's own description of its product; no benchmark or latency data in the paper.
